physical_harm: Death caused by sharp edged weapons
motive: Appellant no.1 wanted utensils from the deceased
key_evidence_accepted: The court accepted the testimony of PW.11, the nephew of the deceased, as a natural witness whose account of the incident was detailed and consistent with other evidence such as the statements of the Investigating Officer (PW.21) and PW.9, the arrest of the accused, and recovery of weapons on their disclosure statements.
witness_credibility: PW.11 was assessed as a trustworthy and natural witness despite being closely related to the deceased. His testimony was found to be reliable even after grilling cross-examination and despite minor discrepancies in witness accounts.
trial_duration: Offence: 5.3.1996; Trial judgment: 21.2.1997; High Court decision: 10.2.2005; Supreme Court decision: 15.12.2006
legal_representation: Siddharth Aggarwal, Aditya Wadhoa, Stui Gujral, Senthil Jagadeesan for the Appellant; Vibha Datta Makhija for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR lodged on 5.3.1996 at 12.30 p.m., charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction upheld; High Court: Conviction upheld; Supreme Court: Appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the two appellants, alongwith another accused, caused the death of PW11's uncle by assaulting him with sharp edged weapons. All the weapons allegedly used in the crime were recovered on the disclosure statements made by the appellants and the other accused. PW.8 conducted post-mortem on the body of the deceased and found three incised wounds on the body, one on the neck, one on the chest and another in the abdomen, all caused by sharp edged weapons. PW11 testified to have witnessed the incident. The prosecution also emphasized that the FIR was lodged promptly and with all details, indicating the truth of the version.
defence_argument: The appellants challenged their conviction on grounds that the ocular evidence was contradictory to the medical evidence as regards the time of death, and that the alleged eye witness PW.11 was closely related to the victim and none of the independent witnesses examined by the prosecution supported its case to the extent that PW.11 could be present on the place of occurrence at the relevant time.
legal_principle_applied: The ocular evidence would have primacy unless it is established that oral evidence is totally irreconcilable with the medical evidence. Where the medical evidence goes so far that it completely rules out all possibility of the ocular evidence if proved, the ocular evidence may be disbelieved.
precedent_relied_upon: State of U.P. v. Hari Chand (2009) 13 SCC 542; Abdul Sayeed v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2010) 10 SCC 259; Bhajan Singh @ Harbhajan Singh & Ors. v. State of Haryana, (2011) 7 SCC 421; Mangu Khan & Ors. v. State of Rajasthan AIR 2005 SC 1912; Baso Prasad & Ors. v. State of Bihar AIR 2007 SC 1019; Kartik Malhar v. State of Bihar (1996) 1 SCC 614; Himanshu @ Chintu v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2011) 2 sec 36; Manju Ram Kalita v. State of Assam (2009) 13 SCC 330; Leela Ram (Dead) thr. Duli Chand v. State of Haryana & Anr. (1999) 9 SCC 525
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because it is improbable that the appellants had been enroped falsely as promptness in lodging the FIR showed that there was no time for manipulation. Prompt and early reporting of the occurrence by the informant with all its vivid details gives an assurance regarding truth of its version.
